subtype: Approach: panic and click a recovery link from an unknown message [Pitfall]
passage:
Day 1. The shopping site's email said a data breach had exposed customer details. Seema read it in the bus queue and her stomach dropped. What if someone emptied her account tonight?

Day 2. A text arrived: "Your account is at risk. To secure it, tap here and send the code we just texted." Her hands were shaking. She tapped, and when the code came, she typed it in without stopping to think.

Day 3. Two payments she never made showed on her statement. Her cousin Vasudha sat beside her while she phoned the bank on the number printed on her card, and the call took two hours. Seema kept repeating, "I was so scared I just did it."

qa.q: What did the text ask Seema to do?
qa.a: It asked her to tap a link and send the code.

qa.q: What was Seema feeling on Day 1 when she read the email in the bus queue?
qa.a: Seema felt panic and dread, her stomach dropping at the thought of losing money.

qa.q: What could Seema do differently next time a message says her account is at risk, and why?
qa.a: She could ignore the link, open the company's own app or number herself, and never share a code, because fear is what makes people act too fast.

qa.q: How might Vasudha see the two hours on the phone?
qa.a: Vasudha may see a worried cousin who needs calm company, and would want to reassure Seema that being tricked while frightened is not stupidity.

grounding: In panic after a breach, the person shares a code from an unknown text asking her to secure the account, and the fraud deepens.

subtype: Approach: panic and click a recovery link from an unknown message [Pitfall]
passage:
Abhinav, you forwarded me that 'secure your account' link and asked if it's real. Good that you asked. Let your Shalini didi tell you what happened when I didn't.
At twenty-one, a shopping site I used emailed me about a breach. I was already rattled, and ten minutes later a text came: 'Account compromised. Click to secure it.' The page looked exactly like the real one. Then a call: a polite man said he'd send an OTP to 'lock' my account, and I should read it back.
I was so scared of losing everything that I didn't think. I read it back. Within an hour, ₹18,000 went from my account to somewhere I've never traced. I reported it to the bank and the cybercrime helpline that day, but the money was gone.
He was calm. I was panicking, and that was what he needed.
So, Abhinav. When something scares you, that is exactly when you slow down. Real companies never ask for your OTP. Close that link and call the number on your card.

qa.q: How much went from Shalini's account?
How did young Shalini feel when the call came?
qa.a: Rattled and scared of losing everything, which stopped her from thinking clearly.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Shalini's story, and what should have happened there?
qa.a: Reading the OTP back to the caller; she should have hung up and called the bank on the number on her card.

qa.q: How might the caller have seen young Shalini's panic?
qa.a: As an opening; the caller stayed calm because her panic made her easy to trick.

grounding: Shows a young person, panicked by a breach notice, following a fake recovery link and sharing an OTP, which deepens the fraud.

subtype: Approach: panic and click a recovery link from an unknown message [Pitfall]
passage:
Siddharth's phone was on four percent, and his train to Nagpur was pulling out, when the breach alert from his food-delivery app came in. Seconds later, a text: 'Suspicious login detected. Secure your wallet now,' with a link.
Heart pounding, battery dying, he tapped it. The page asked for his phone number, then: 'Enter the OTP we've sent to confirm it's you.' An OTP arrived. He typed it in without reading the message it came with.
The phone died.
When Hrithik lent him a charger two hours later, there were six new messages from his bank. ₹9,500 had gone from his account, in three payments to a wallet he'd never heard of. The OTP message he had rushed past had said, in plain words, 'OTP for payment of ₹3,000. Do not share.'
Hrithik sat beside him. 'Call the bank's number on your card. Now. Then the cybercrime helpline.' Siddharth did both before the train reached Itarsi, hands shaking. The bank blocked the account, but the money was already gone.

qa.q: How much had gone from Siddharth's account?
What was Siddharth feeling when he tapped the link?
qa.a: Panicked, heart pounding, rushed by the dying battery and the frightening alert.

qa.q: What could Siddharth have done when the alert and text came?
qa.a: Ignored the link, waited until he could call the bank on the number on his card, and never shared an OTP.

qa.q: How might Hrithik feel seeing the messages?
qa.a: Concerned for his friend but steady, pushing him to call the bank and the helpline straight away.

grounding: Shows a young person panicking after a breach alert, clicking an unknown link and entering an OTP, which lets the fraud deepen.
